clue.text: Singer’s tense after news in story

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a story can be a fib or untruth
N is short for new, so news is read as two of them
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A nervous vocalist is on edge after some bad news appears in a newspaper story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer’s tense' reads as a nervous performer, but the possessive is 'Singer is', and tense is only the grammar letter. Reading news as two Ns (plural of new) is a convention worth learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A linnet is a small finch prized for its song, so any songbird counts as a singer in crosswords.

clue.text: Large fish starts to occupy Pacific after hurricane

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so we keep only the front of each word that follows

blocks.note: the first letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A huge fish begins to settle in the Pacific once a hurricane has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to occupy' looks like a verb phrase about the fish moving in; it actually tells you to take the initial letter of each of the next four words.
explanation.definitionFit: The opah, or moonfish, is a big brightly coloured ocean species that can weigh over a hundred pounds.

clue.text: Scientist’s way in blocking Schrödinger’s articles

indicators.note: something put in a gap to block it sits between the pieces on either side

blocks.note: ein is the German indefinite article, the language of the Austrian physicist Schrödinger; two of them
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A physicist’s route into Schrödinger’s published papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests scientific papers, but here it means grammatical articles in German, the language of Schrödinger, the Austrian physicist.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein, the physicist behind relativity, is perhaps the most famous scientist of all.

clue.text: Formerly bombards river in Staffordshire

definitions.note: STRAFF is an old variant spelling of strafe, hence 'Formerly'

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: Staffs is the standard abbreviation for this English Midlands county
R is the usual abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A wartime memory of aircraft once attacking a river in the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Staffordshire is a county in central England, abbreviated STAFFS; R goes inside after ST to give STRAFFS, an older spelling of strafes.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack with gunfire from low-flying aircraft; STRAFF is an earlier spelling recorded in dictionaries.

clue.text: Move quietly and tilt from West?

blocks.note: to tilt something is to tip it
heading away from the west means going to the east, written TO E

explanation.surface: Someone creeps along softly while leaning over from the western side.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful reading: tilting from the west is tilting towards the east, TIP TO E.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking on the balls of the feet is the classic way to creep about without making noise.

clue.text: Past master in reconstructing special valves

indicators.note: reconstructing means building again from the same parts in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An expert craftsman restoring some unusual valves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Past master' reads as an expert, but its ten letters are the raw material, rebuilt to make the two-word answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam traps are automatic devices fitted to pipework that let condensed water out while holding the steam in.

clue.text: Number in mileage initially ignored, for example

indicators.note: ignoring the start of a word means dropping its opening letter
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for number
mileage is distance travelled; its first letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A figure on the milometer that was overlooked at first, say.
explanation.walkthrough: DISTANCE loses its D to leave ISTANCE, and N slips in after the I to make INSTANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case or illustration, the same thing as an example; 'for example' and 'for instance' are interchangeable phrases.

clue.text: Precisely determine security code and give directions

blocks.note: a PIN is a personal identification number used for bank cards
to show someone the way you point

explanation.surface: Work out the exact access code and tell people how to get there.
explanation.walkthrough: Two everyday words placed side by side: the code typed at a cash machine, then the gesture of indicating direction.
explanation.definitionFit: To pinpoint something is to locate or identify it with great accuracy, as if marking it with a pin.

clue.text: Start and end of time in pub - time having particular purpose

indicators.note: the start and end of a word are its two outside letters
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: an inn is a pub
the first and last letters of the word
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Closing time at the bar, when drinking takes on a determined purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time' appears twice: first trimmed to its outer letters and tucked inside INN, then as the plain abbreviation T added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Being intent on something means being resolved or set upon a goal, so the adjective describes someone with a fixed aim.

clue.text: Wavering, hesitant, us? I’ll plunge straight in

indicators.note: something wavering is unsteady and shifting, so these letters move about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Speaking to the timid and doubtful, someone announces they will dive right in.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole spoken line, a self-description; the contrast with the hesitant fodder is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: An eager devotee throws themself into an activity without hesitation, which is exactly what the speaker claims to do.

clue.text: A Southern Italian recalled Italian town

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so this element is brought back the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for southern
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: Someone from the south of Italy remembers a small town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern Italian' looks like one person; it splits into S and IT, with IT turned round. Gin and it is a British cocktail of gin and Italian vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a town in Piedmont, northern Italy, famous for its sparkling wine.

clue.text: Suppress steps to restrain France

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold something in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a stile is a set of steps for climbing over a fence
F is the international vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: Measures taken to hold back France sound like diplomatic policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steps' looks like measures or actions; it is the countryside stile, a set of steps over a wall or fence, holding F.
explanation.definitionFit: To stifle a yawn or a protest is to hold it back, the same as suppressing it.

clue.text: Cleaner to baffle the clergy

blocks.note: to floor someone is to baffle or stump them
the cloth is a collective term for the clergy

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady sets out to confound the local priests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' suggests a person who cleans; it is an object. 'The cloth' as a name for clergy comes from their distinctive dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A floorcloth is a rag used for wiping and mopping floors, so it is a cleaning item.

clue.text: Get away with money - $1000 - taking almost no time

blocks.note: to flee is to get away
tin is old slang for money
G stands for grand, a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: A robber makes off with a thousand dollars in the blink of an eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface looks like a quick heist; the pieces simply run in order. Grand, written G, is slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fleeting is brief and passing quickly, lasting only an instant.

clue.text: Troublesome term for student wanting sex?

blocks.note: T is a dictionary abbreviation for term
slang for someone feeling sexual desire

explanation.surface: A tricky question: what do you call a randy undergraduate?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a cheeky reading; 'term' is not a word for something but just its abbreviation T, followed by the slang adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorny problem is one full of difficulties, prickly like a briar, hence troublesome.

clue.text: Shade given to a hair application comes from Cornish location

blocks.note: a tint is a shade of colour
taken as written
gel is a styling product put on hair

explanation.surface: A hair colour applied with a product is advertised as coming from Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like salon talk; 'given to' just strings the pieces in order. Cornwall is the county at the far south-west tip of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Tintagel is a village on the north Cornish coast, famous for its ruined castle linked to King Arthur.

clue.text: Relaxed when in a casual shirt

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: taken as written
a tee is a T-shirt
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Feeling comfortable when dressed down in a T-shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene is so coherent that 'when' passes as a plain conjunction; it is a piece of wordplay meaning 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: At ease is an idiom for comfortable and unworried, also the military order to stand relaxed.

clue.text: Article about one actual crime

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: the definite article
Roman numeral one
very in the sense of 'the very thing', real or actual

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about a real criminal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a news story; it is the grammatical article, and 'actual' is the sense in 'the very thing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thievery is the act of stealing, a specific kind of crime.

clue.text: Seal off to seal, I fancy

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamental, so these letters are dressed up in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone considers closing something off by sealing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I fancy' reads as 'I think'; 'fancy' is the signal and 'I' joins the letters. The repeated 'seal' looks clumsy but one is definition, one fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To isolate an area or patient is to cut it off from contact, keeping everything else out.

clue.text: Fixes cocktail of gin with quantities of water?

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so these letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
rains are falls of water

explanation.surface: A bartender fixes a drink by watering down the gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixes' looks like mixing drinks, and 'cocktail' seems to continue that bar scene; the question mark admits rains are a loose kind of quantity of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingrain a habit or stain is to fix it deeply and firmly so it cannot be removed.

clue.text: I prevent artist showing city in Ecuador

blocks.note: taken as written
to bar is to prevent
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: Someone stops a painter from exhibiting a South American city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests censoring a painting; the pieces simply join in order. RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibarra is a city in the northern Andes of Ecuador, capital of Imbabura province.

clue.text: Fit? I note revolution in muscles

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so these letters face the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
N is short for note
lats are the latissimus dorsi muscles of the back

explanation.surface: Feeling healthy, a gym-goer notices a turning motion in the muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit?' looks like an adjective for health; it is a verb, meaning set up. INSTAL is the British spelling with one L.
explanation.definitionFit: To instal a device is to fit it in place, put it in position ready for use.

clue.text: Sour spies snatching private eye in upset

indicators.note: to snatch is to grab and hold, so one piece takes another inside it
to upset is to turn over, and in a down clue that flips the order

blocks.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency
tec is short for detective

explanation.surface: Bitter agents kidnap a detective amid turmoil.
explanation.walkthrough: CIA holds TEC to make CITECA, and the whole is then flipped upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetic means relating to vinegar, whose acetic acid gives it a sharp, sour taste.

clue.text: Remarkable count, but falling short

indicators.note: falling short means not reaching the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: a tally is a count

explanation.surface: An impressive count that nevertheless misses the target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkable' as a definition is fair through the phrase 'a tall story', one hard to believe.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall tale or tall order is extraordinary or hard to credit, so tall can mean remarkable in that sense.

clue.text: Everything takes a new direction after ditching first cushions

indicators.note: ditching the first means throwing away the opening letter

blocks.note: everything is all
to deviate is to turn off course

explanation.surface: After abandoning its leader, everything heads off another way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cushions' at the end looks like a noun; it is a verb, and the first letter ditched belongs to the verb for changing course, not to 'Everything'.
explanation.definitionFit: To cushion a blow is to soften its impact, just as alleviating pain lessens it.

clue.text: Expression of sympathy over a year on holiday

blocks.note: aw is a sympathetic exclamation
taken as written
Y is short for year

explanation.surface: Someone sends condolences after a whole year off on vacation.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' places the first piece above the next ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is away is absent from home, as people are on vacation.

clue.text: Phi half backed this examiner

indicators.note: backing half means turning just one part round so it runs the other way

blocks.note: Phi is the pseudonym of this puzzle's compiler

explanation.surface: The puzzle's compiler, half-heartedly supported, becomes an examiner.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by pseudonym: Phi is the setter of this puzzle, and only the first half of that word is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A tester checks or assesses something, which is the job of any examiner; a puzzle setter tests solvers too.

clue.text: Seabird about to strike one reptile

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a tern is a seabird
to rap is to strike sharply
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A gull swoops about to attack a lizard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to strike' reads as poised to attack; 'about' actually tells the bird to wrap round the next pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrapin is a small freshwater turtle, and turtles are reptiles.
